citation: Yip PSF, Law CK, Fu KW, Law YW, Wong PWC, Xu Y. Restricting the means of suicide by charcoal burning. British Journal of Psychiatry. 2010;196:241–242. doi:10.1192/bjp.bp.109.065185.
title: Restricting the means of suicide by charcoal burning
abstract: Exploratory controlled community trial comparing a Hong Kong district where barbecue charcoal was removed from open retail shelves with a control district where charcoal remained openly displayed.
population: residents of Tuen Mun and Yuen Long, Hong Kong
intervention_or_exposure: restricted retail access to barbecue charcoal
comparator: usual open-shelf charcoal display in control district

effect_estimates.measure: Tuen Mun rate per 100,000 before→during intervention
Tuen Mun rate per 100,000 before→during intervention
Yuen Long control rate per 100,000 before→during intervention

uncertainty: Exploratory district-level controlled trial rather than an individually randomized trial.
Potential contextual differences between districts may remain despite controlled comparisons.
methods: Poisson regression adjusted for age and gender

evidence_claims.statement: During the 12-month intervention, the charcoal-burning suicide rate in Tuen Mun fell from 4.3 to 2.0 per 100,000 (a 53.5% reduction), while the control district increased from 3.0 to 4.3 per 100,000.
evidence_claims.population: residents of Tuen Mun and Yuen Long, Hong Kong
evidence_claims.intervention_or_exposure: restricted retail access to barbecue charcoal

provenance.locator: British Journal of Psychiatry short report, Results, p. 241
provenance.source_span: The report gives pre/post district rates and percentage changes for charcoal-burning suicide.

evidence_claims.statement: The all-method suicide rate in Tuen Mun fell from 17.9 to 12.2 per 100,000 (31.8%), compared with a 1.6% reduction in Yuen Long.
evidence_claims.population: residents of Tuen Mun and Yuen Long, Hong Kong
evidence_claims.intervention_or_exposure: restricted retail access to barbecue charcoal

provenance.locator: British Journal of Psychiatry short report, Results, p. 241
provenance.source_span: The report compares all-method suicide-rate changes in intervention and control districts.

evidence_claims.statement: The study did not observe a significant increase in suicide by other methods, providing no clear evidence of method substitution during the intervention period.
evidence_claims.population: residents of Tuen Mun and Yuen Long, Hong Kong
evidence_claims.intervention_or_exposure: restricted retail access to barbecue charcoal

provenance.locator: British Journal of Psychiatry, Summary and Methods
provenance.source_span: The authors report no significant change in suicide using other methods and explicitly tested for method substitution.

limitations: Community-level exploratory design, not individual randomization.
Results come from two Hong Kong districts and may depend on local retail and method-use patterns.
Short report provides limited detail compared with a full-scale trial report.
applicability: Supports evaluation of population-level means-restriction strategies in contexts where charcoal burning is a common suicide method.
Requires local adaptation before transfer to settings with different means patterns or retail systems.
safety_boundaries: Do not interpret community-level rate changes as an individual treatment effect.
This evidence supports population prevention policy, not instructions concerning methods of self-harm.
